article_title: Dropout Prevention
citation: Prevention Science in School Settings chapter, edited by Kris Bosworth. (2015). Dropout Prevention: A Previously Intractable Problem Addressed Through Systems for Monitoring and Supporting Students. Springer. https://www.springer.com
title: Develop school policies and practices that prevent struggle and make supportive staff-student relationships easier to establish
description: The chapter holds that dropout prevention is not only about reacting to risk but about shaping school conditions: "Schools can develop policies and practices that make it less likely students will struggle in school, and that make it easier for school staff to establish supportive relationships with students." Prevention-oriented school design thus combines structural policy with relational support for students in the early high school years.
requirements: School staff capacity to establish supportive relationships with students
examples: School-level systems in Chicago for using data to identify which students need what types of support

article_title: Scaling Career Pathways Statewide: A Blueprint for Creating K-12 + Postsecondary + Industry Pathways
citation: Scaling career pathways statewide: A blueprint for creating K-12 + postsecondary + industry pathways. (2026). Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/287
title: State and regional policy levers drive cross-sector coherence for pathways scale-up
description: The blueprint argues that policy is the galvanizing mechanism for scale. It states: "State and regional policy levers are core incentives and accelerants to K-12 statewide pathways. Policies set the conditions for scaling by creating a centralized galvanizing mechanism that drives coherence across K-12, postsecondary and industry." What must be true includes a champion at the statehouse, a lead statewide backbone implementation organization, policy conditions enabling innovation such as teacher accelerated certification and micro-credentials, and interoperable policy, data, and practice infrastructure.
requirements: A champion at the statehouse or influencer leader within the state
a lead statewide backbone implementation organization
interoperable policy, data, and practice infrastructure and systems
constraints: The article notes gaps where incentive structures for K-12 and industry are at odds must be addressed
target_learning_goals: scaled access to career-connected pathways and credentials
examples: The ACTIVATE pillar's strategic questions ask what shared definition of statewide pathways success incentivizes regions, districts, and communities

article_title: Portraits in Progress: Emerging Future-Ready Skills Assessment Strategies
citation: Kyle Dunbar, Katie Wilczak, Kelly Mills, Nick Mireles, and Alison Shell. (2025). Portraits in Progress: Emerging Future-Ready Skills Assessment Strategies. Digital Promise and Pearson. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Three-component framework for Portrait of a Graduate assessment systems
description: The report defines assessment as the process of gathering, analyzing, and interpreting evidence of student learning, and organizes district activity into three components: collecting evidence, evaluating and analyzing that evidence, and reporting and communicating student growth. District methods are mapped onto this framework in Figure 1 and Table 1, spanning performance tasks, tech-enabled scenarios, defenses of learning, rubrics, self-reflection, report cards, microcredentials, and dashboards.

constraints: The framework is drawn from a landscape scan of districts at different stages of Portrait of a Graduate implementation, not from a validated measurement study
target_learners: K-12 students in districts with Portrait of a Graduate frameworks
target_learning_goals: future-ready skills such as critical thinking, communication, collaboration, and creativity
examples: District strategies organized by assessment component observed in the landscape scan, per Figure 1 and Table 1

citation: Kyle Dunbar, Katie Wilczak, Kelly Mills, Nick Mireles, and Alison Shell. (2025). Portraits in Progress: Emerging Future-Ready Skills Assessment Strategies. Digital Promise and Pearson. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Badging with physical Badge Books and 'I can' statements (South Glens Falls)
description: Badging is a reporting method in which badges—visuals representing specific skills—are awarded when students demonstrate proficiency, physically or digitally. In South Glens Falls, students earn badges in a physical Badge Book of stickers that includes "I can…" statements for each skill, awarded by teachers, principals, and district leaders using district-level criteria. The report notes badges generate student excitement but, without valid measures, may not be awarded consistently and comparably.
requirements: Valid measures and strong systems, plus a process by which students receive an explanation of why they did or did not earn a badge
constraints: Best used as part of a wider system of assessment with careful thought to collecting and evaluating student evidence
target_learners: K-12 students in districts using badging
examples: Three districts interviewed are experimenting with badging as a means of communicating student achievement

article_title: The Educational Attainment of Chicago Public Schools Students (2024)
citation: Mahaffie, S., Usher, A., Nagaoka, J., & McKoy, D. (2025). The Educational Attainment of Chicago Public Schools Students: 2024. To&Through Project and UChicago Consortium on School Research. https://toandthrough.uchicago.edu/
title: Post-secondary Attainment Index
description: The report combines its three milestone rates into what authors call a "Post-secondary Attainment Index". It expresses attainment as a hypothetical cohort trajectory: "if 100 students started CPS in ninth grade today, 84 would graduate high school, 58 would enroll immediately in college, and 30 would complete a college credential within 10 years." The index turns graduation, enrollment, and completion rates into a single composite indicator for tracking progress over time.
requirements: Requires data on high school graduation, immediate college enrollment, and college credential completion for CPS cohorts
constraints: The completion component reflects rates for cohorts for which six years of post-secondary data exist, such as the class of 2018
target_learners: Chicago Public Schools students starting ninth grade
target_learning_goals: High school graduation, immediate college enrollment, and college credential completion
examples: The 2024 report expresses the index as 84 of 100 students graduating high school, 58 enrolling immediately in college, and 30 completing a credential within 10 years

article_title: The Educational Attainment of Chicago Public Schools Students (2023)
citation: Mahaffie, S., Usher, A., Nagaoka, J., & McKoy, D. (2024). The educational attainment of Chicago Public Schools students: 2023. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://toandthrough.uchicago.edu/tool/cps/
title: Post-secondary Attainment Index (PAI)
description: The Post-secondary Attainment Index is a district-level summary measure representing "the proportion of current CPS ninth-graders who would complete any degree or certificate from a two-year or four-year college within 10 years" if current rates held. It multiplies the four-year graduation rate by a weighted combination of enrollment and completion rates for four-year enrollees, two-year enrollees, and non-enrollees, combining data from multiple recent cohorts. The 2023 PAI synthesizes graduation data for the class of 2023, enrollment data for the class of 2023, and six-year college outcomes for the class of 2017.
requirements: Requires four-year high school graduation rates, immediate college enrollment rates, and six-year college completion rates, each from the most recent available cohort
constraints: Not a true cohort attainment rate; it does not follow one single cohort for 10 consecutive years and is not intended as a prediction of what will happen
target_learners: CPS ninth-graders and high school students
target_learning_goals: District-level monitoring of high school graduation, college enrollment, and college completion attainment
examples: The 2023 PAI of 30.6% combines the class of 2023 graduation rate, class of 2023 immediate enrollment rates, and class of 2017 six-year completion rates

article_title: So, You Want to Create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and Considerations for the Field
citation: Terrell, J. H., Ahigian, R., Garvey, M., & Barzee, S. (2025). So, you want to create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and considerations for the field. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Governance taxonomy of POG development and implementation approaches varying by state involvement and local autonomy
description: The brief organizes POG development and implementation along a governance axis: "Approaches for developing and implementing POGs vary widely across states and districts, including the level of state involvement and local autonomy." It distinguishes a state-led standardized approach (e.g., Indiana, North Carolina, Virginia) that "ensures a level of consistency" from locally controlled approaches (e.g., California, Colorado, Illinois, Iowa) that allow customization, and notes most states do not mandate a POG at all, in which case districts may mandate and develop their own.
requirements: States or districts must decide how local goals align with or diverge from state policies, consulting the state department of education particularly on assessment and accountability requirements.
constraints: The brief states the locally controlled approach "can also lead to a diverse patchwork of graduate profiles," creating consistency challenges, while the state-led approach must balance "statewide consistency and the need for local relevance."
target_learning_goals: demonstrating knowledge, skills, and abilities to graduate and contribute to families, workplaces, and communities
examples: States such as Indiana, North Carolina, and Virginia adopted a standardized state-developed POG; California, Colorado, Illinois, and Iowa provide districts flexibility to develop their own POGs.
key_sources: Terrell, J. H., Ahigian, R., Garvey, M., & Barzee, S. (2025). So, you want to create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and considerations for the field. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED673579

article_title: So, You Want to Create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and Considerations for the Field
citation: Terrell, J. H., Ahigian, R., Garvey, M., & Barzee, S. (2025). So, you want to create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and considerations for the field. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Establish a representative design committee and limit POG competencies to six or fewer
description: The brief recommends a design committee including representatives from state and local businesses and nonprofits, school and district leadership, students, and families, which creates, vets, and refines the competency list and outlines a high-level vision serving as the educational North Star. Researchers and practitioners recommend limiting competencies to six or fewer because "the power of a POG lies in its ability to align and focus educators." Common competencies include durable skills such as communication, critical thinking, and leadership.
requirements: A design committee with diverse interest-holder representation; third-party organizations are often engaged to facilitate feedback sessions and summarize information for the committee.
target_learning_goals: defining and focusing instruction on durable skills and behavioral regulation competencies
examples: Core competencies most commonly reflected in POGs include communication, critical thinking, and leadership, with personal and interpersonal competencies such as creativity, adaptability, persistence, and relational awareness often included.

citation: Terrell, J. H., Ahigian, R., Garvey, M., & Barzee, S. (2025). So, you want to create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and considerations for the field. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Centralized online POG resource hub with advisory-group curation
description: Following assessment decisions, states and districts can support educators by creating a centralized resource hub offering guidelines and exemplars for effective assessment implementation. States like Colorado, New Hampshire, Utah, and Virginia have created online platforms where educators and administrators can access resources, share experiences, and learn from successful POG implementations. State and industry leaders can recruit a state POG advisory group to vet resources and tools and regularly convene to improve the site.
requirements: The hub should be regularly updated with new materials and case studies from districts and other states; an advisory group should regularly convene to discuss, improve, and bring fresh ideas and innovations to the site.
examples: Colorado, New Hampshire, Utah, and Virginia created an online platform or hub for educators and administrators to access resources and share experiences.

article_title: So, You Want to Create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and Considerations for the Field
citation: Terrell, J. H., Ahigian, R., Garvey, M., & Barzee, S. (2025). So, you want to create a Portrait of a Graduate? Factors and considerations for the field. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Translate POG competencies into measurable objectives aligned with state standards to guide teaching and assessment
description: The brief recommends that states and districts develop clear assessment criteria and align POG competencies with state standards. By translating competencies into measurable objectives, educators receive a clear roadmap for both teaching and evaluating the competencies, enabling assessments to serve as a guide for continuous instructional improvement. Alignment is fostered through collaboration among state education departments, district leaders, teachers, higher education institutions, and industry experts.
requirements: Collaborative efforts between state education departments, district leaders, teachers, institutions of higher education, and industry experts to ensure POG assessments reflect the rigor and quality of state standards.
constraints: Districts may struggle to balance POG competency assessments with state-mandated standardized tests, and may lack resources for time- and resource-intensive performance tasks, portfolios, and project-based learning evaluations.
target_learning_goals: teaching and evaluating POG competencies within the broader educational system
examples: Some states align standardized testing with POG competencies through crosswalks of state standards, revising test items for higher order thinking, or incorporating performance-based tasks in areas like communication and collaboration.

article_title: Making Dual Enrollment Work: Solving the Access-Success Paradox with OUSD's Point Person Model
citation: Terrell, J. H., Mathias, J., Roldan-Rueda, D., & Blanchard, A. (2026). Making dual enrollment work: Solving the access–success paradox with OUSD’s point person model. WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: The Point Person: an embedded OUSD staff member supporting each dual enrollment classroom
description: The point person is an OUSD staff member—typically a classroom teacher, occasionally a counselor or other school employee—embedded in every dual enrollment classroom alongside the Peralta instructor. The role is defined by six functions: the point person "is present during college instruction alongside the Peralta instructor," holds the classroom on off days, monitors progress through the college's learning management system, coordinates interventions, bridges communication between instructor, students, staff, and families, and manages logistics. The model evolved organically over 11 years of problem-solving rather than from research or policy mandates, and was then systematized.
requirements: Point people must know the students, understand high school culture, and can convey differences between college expectations and adolescent learners' realities
constraints: Funding arrangements vary by site with no single formula; the report notes floating-staff arrangements result in less relationship continuity
target_learners: High school students in dual enrollment courses, predominantly first-generation students, students from low-income backgrounds, and students of color
target_learning_goals: College course success and pass rates in dual enrollment coursework
examples: In every OUSD dual enrollment classroom the point person sits alongside the Peralta instructor, holds off-day sessions, checks Canvas gradebooks weekly, and coordinates interventions for struggling students.

article_title: Access to Powerful Technology as a Catalyst for Career Pathway Engagement
citation: Wortman, A., and Schiner, N. (2024, June). Access to powerful technology as a catalyst for career pathway engagement [Project Report]. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/217
title: Powerful learning principles: personal and accessible, authentic and challenging, collaborative and connected, inquisitive and reflective
description: The paper defines powerful learning as "a set of principles that guide educators to design learning experiences that meaningfully engage students": "personal and accessible, authentic and challenging, collaborative and connected, and inquisitive and reflective." The HP Learning Studio is presented as exemplifying these: it is centrally located and not tied to one class, supports authentic community-serving projects, enables collaborative creation of shareable learning artifacts, and fosters a safe space to fail and iterate. requirements: A centrally located, shared space not tied to any one teacher's class or club, so access is open to all students and educators
constraints: The paper notes multiple studies support the motivating character of authentic project-based environments, but the studio's own instantiation is documented only through qualitative examples
target_learners: high school students, particularly historically and systemically excluded youth
target_learning_goals: meaningful engagement, passion and interest discovery, preparation for future careers
examples: Students created products as learning artifacts shared locally or globally; Mr. Duarte's client-based website project exemplified collaborative and connected learning

article_title: Accountability for Postsecondary Readiness. A 50-State Analysis
citation: Mitchell P. Herz, Lamar L. Johnson, and Eric W. Crane. (2023). Accountability for Postsecondary Readiness: A 50-State Analysis. Region 15 Comprehensive Center at WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Three-type taxonomy of postsecondary readiness measures: academic, career, and military
description: The brief organizes the measures states use in postsecondary readiness indicators into three types. As the authors state, "Three main types of measures were identified: academic, career, and military." Academic measures include advanced course completion, SAT/ACT thresholds, on-track-to-graduate status, advanced diplomas, multilingual certificates, and college enrollment or remediation. Career measures include industry credentials, CTE course completion, work-based learning, and WorkKeys thresholds. Military measures include ASVAB thresholds or enlistment. The taxonomy emerged from coding the measures across all ESSA plans.
requirements: States must define which specific measures count within each type in their ESSA plans; where plans lacked detail, state agency websites were consulted.
constraints: The taxonomy reflects only measures documented in federally approved ESSA plans as of May 1, 2023.
target_learning_goals: postsecondary readiness for college, career, and military pathways
examples: Pennsylvania's plan used the Career Standards Benchmark as its sole postsecondary readiness measure; North Dakota's plan included 23 separate measures.

citation: Misan Paul Etchie, Olutosin Taiwo. (2026). AI-Integrated Learning Management System for Middle School: A Longitudinal Study of Learning Outcomes Through High School and Beyond. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.07544
title: Gate AI assistance for minors through a policy gateway with privacy-first governance and audit logs
description: For deployment with minors, the article treats governance and privacy as first-class architectural requirements. All help requests pass through a policy gateway where 'the gateway evaluates classroom policy and task context, applying rules such as age-appropriate constraints, content filters, and assessment-specific restrictions'; disallowed or violating outputs are blocked and replaced with safe fallbacks. Separation of personally identifiable information from de-identified research logs
Continuous safety monitoring of AI outputs with a process for correcting or disabling harmful behaviors

examples: Parents/guardians view high-level progress summaries without access to sensitive details or AI chat logs; audit logs capture AI prompts/responses, gateway policy decisions, and teacher overrides

article_title: EducaSim: Interactive Simulacra for CS1 Instructional Practice
citation: Cameron Mohne, Nicholas Vo, Dora Demszky, Chris Piech. (2026). EducaSim: Interactive Simulacra for CS1 Instructional Practice. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.11444
title: Post-session feedback combining talktime statistics, LLM analysis, and self-reflection prompts
description: EducaSim's feedback pattern layers three components after each session: talktime statistics totaling each speaker's words and silence; LLM-generated feedback identifying instructional behaviors such as teacher uptake, talk proportions, questioning quality, and evidence of student misconceptions; and reflective prompts for teacher self-assessment. A separate LLM infers reasons behind instructional challenges, selects remediation strategies, and highlights what the teacher did well, such as "answering questions, revoicing student understandings, or attempts at engaging students".
requirements: Requires a full session transcript of teacher-student interaction to analyze
constraints: Feedback effectiveness depends on the teacher's uptake; the pattern was designed for CS1 small-group scenarios
target_learning_goals: Improving instructional behaviors such as uptake, questioning, and student engagement
examples: One teacher reported reviewing the feedback and changing her approach, which produced more student replies in her second session

article_title: Family-school autonomy support for children's responsible use of generative artificial intelligence
citation: Fan Y, Li X and Zhang R (2026). Family-school autonomy support for children's responsible use of generative artificial intelligence: a self-determination theory synthesis and developmental research agenda. Front. Psychol. 17:1969217. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1969217
title: Pair clear GenAI policy boundaries with autonomy support rather than choosing between control and permissiveness
description: The review argues against a false choice between unrestricted autonomy and technological control, holding that "Clarity is most likely to support integrity when rules specify acceptable assistance, explain why boundaries matter, offer practice in disclosure and verification, and preserve meaningful choice within those boundaries." In SDT terms, autonomy support and structure are separable dimensions, and detection or punishment alone cannot cultivate judgment. The principle integrates transparent boundaries with AI literacy, reflective-use training, process-oriented assessment, and disclosure practice.
requirements: Rules that specify acceptable assistance and explain why boundaries matter
Practice in disclosure and verification
Meaningful choice preserved within the boundaries
constraints: Students in nursing education report insufficient guidance about acceptable GenAI use, so clarity alone may not reach learners without delivery
target_learners: children and adolescents using generative AI in learning
examples: The review cites process-aware pedagogy, source verification, citation skills, and redesigned assessments as ways to make standards actionable, and a student-partnered Delphi study producing 14 consensus principles for responsible GenAI use in medical education
key_sources: Fan Y, Li X and Zhang R (2026). Family-school autonomy support for children's responsible use of generative artificial intelligence: a self-determination theory synthesis and developmental research agenda. Front. Psychol. 17:1969217. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1969217

article_title: When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution
citation: Kai Yao. (2026). When AI Does the Work, What Is Learning For? Post-Instrumental Learning and the Risk of Capacity Dissolution. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28041
title: Post-instrumental learning: formation of capacities needed for agency and accountability under extensive AI delegation
description: Post-instrumental learning is the article's central framework: the formation of capacities that remain necessary for agency, responsibility, and meaning when many products of learning can be delegated to AI. It is defined as "the formation of capacities that remain necessary for agency, responsibility, and meaning under extensive AI delegation". The term does not deny learning's instrumental value; it marks a shift in emphasis, from whether people must produce outputs unaided to whether they retain the capacities to set ends, ask for reasons, contest decisions, refuse harmful dependence, revise practices, and participate in the forms of life AI helps mediate.
requirements: Delegated work must remain connected to purposes, reasons, alternatives, and repair through people, intermediaries, and institutions
constraints: The account is a normative conceptual analysis, not an empirical measurement of learning loss or a design proposal for one educational technology
target_learners: citizens affected by AI-mediated institutional practices
target_learning_goals: preserving capacities for agency, responsibility, and accountability under AI delegation

article_title: Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgment visible
citation: Sunaina Sharma. (2026). Educational integrity in GenAI-augmented assessment: making judgement visible. International Journal for Educational Integrity 22:6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40979-026-00216-y
title: Postplagiarism as an educational integrity framework reframing integrity around responsibility rather than control
description: The paper adopts Eaton's postplagiarism as a lens for rethinking educational integrity in GenAI-augmented contexts, recognizing hybrid human-GenAI writing as a contemporary condition of academic work. It states that postplagiarism "does not abandon integrity standards; it reframes them around responsibility rather than control", so integrity is defined not by whether GenAI was used but by how decisions were justified and disclosed. The paper extends this ethical orientation into structural assessment design.
requirements: Assessment design and institutional policy must support integrity as an enacted ethical practice rather than enforce it technologically
constraints: The framework addresses GenAI-augmented academic work in which responsibility for academic decisions remains with the human author
target_learning_goals: ethical academic practice and responsible GenAI use
examples: The paper operationalizes postplagiarism through four illustrative assessment practices that foreground transparency, justification, and accountability

citation: Janos Perczel, Jin Chow, and Dorottya Demszky. (2025). TeachLM: Post-Training LLMs for Education Using Authentic Learning Data. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.05087
title: Polygence authentic learning dataset of over 100,000 hours of one-on-one tutoring interactions
description: A large longitudinal dataset of one-on-one, project-based tutoring sessions between PhD-level tutors and students across more than 150 subjects, collected through the Polygence platform. The article states it "comprises more than 100,000 hours of one-on-one, longitudinal student–tutor interactions in multiple modalities," including meeting transcripts, shared documents, and chat. It was anonymized on internal servers and used for post-training and benchmarking LLMs for education.
requirements: Recorded sessions require explicit participant consent with real-time notification of recording
Data processing must honor participant opt-outs and undergo anonymization to remove PII
constraints: Data was curated consistent with the platform's terms of use and privacy policy; anonymization removed tutor identity, personal background, and personal opinions before training

target_learning_goals: Project-based research and creative projects across STEM and Humanities subjects

article_title: A Posthumanist Approach to AI Literacy
citation: Zhaozhe Wang, Chaoran Wang. (2025). A posthumanist approach to AI literacy. Computers and Composition 76 (2025) 102933. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compcom.2025.102933
title: A posthumanist approach to AI literacy: meaning emerges through human-AI intra-actions
description: This framework reframes AI literacy away from anthropocentric models in which humans use AI tools toward meaning-making. Drawing on Barad, Latour, Bennett, and Deleuze and Guattari, it holds that agency is distributed and enacted through intra-actions of human agents and non-human actants. As the authors put it, it "frames AI literacy as an understanding of how meaning emerges through human-AI intra-actions." Literacy with AI is thus relational work rather than transactional work, extending the New Literacy Studies' situated-practices view to include AI actancy.
requirements: Educators and students must develop meta-awareness of AI-mediated ways of meaning-making across AI-charged, AI-free, and in-between contexts
constraints: The authors caution against corporate anthropomorphism, e.g. discourse that AI boosts productivity, which shapes a transactional view of human-AI relations
target_learning_goals: understanding distributed agency in AI-mediated meaning-making
examples: The authors analyzed two students' AI-assisted writing through the lenses of conceptualization, positionality, intra-actions, and evaluation of AI affordances

article_title: The evaluation of physical learning environments: a critical review of the literature
citation: Benjamin Cleveland & Kenn Fisher. (2014). The evaluation of physical learning environments: a critical review of the literature. Learning Environ Res 17, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10984-013-9149-3
title: Post-occupancy evaluation as a developed methodology for evaluating non-domestic buildings
description: Post-occupancy evaluation (POE) is presented as an established methodology for evaluating non-domestic buildings, which the review charts historically to contextualize learning-space evaluation. The authors write that "we initially chart the development of post-occupancy evaluation (POE) for non-domestic buildings." POE serves as the foundational evaluative tradition from which the later, broader building performance evaluation framework emerged, and the review treats its development as the starting point for understanding how learning environments have been evaluated.
requirements: Buildings that are occupied and in use, so that performance after occupancy can be evaluated
constraints: Originally developed for non-domestic buildings rather than specifically for learning environments
target_learners: Students in school and higher education physical learning environments
target_learning_goals: Evaluating whether physical learning environments support intended educational activities

article_title: Mad City Mystery: Developing Scientific Argumentation Skills with a Place-based Augmented Reality Game on Handheld Computers
citation: Squire, K.D., Jan, M. (2007). Mad City Mystery: Developing Scientific Argumentation Skills with a Place-based Augmented Reality Game on Handheld Computers. J Sci Educ Technol 16, 5–29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10956-006-9037-z
title: Post-progressive pedagogy through narrative game play: developing narrative accounts of scientific phenomena as a mechanism for scientific argumentation
description: The article proposes that location-based augmented reality games can create a "post-progressive" pedagogy in which students are immersed in authentic scientific inquiry and required to perform in adult scientific discourses. Its core mechanism is that "Through game play, players are required to develop narrative accounts of scientific phenomena, a process that requires them to develop and argue scientific explanations." Game features then scaffold this thinking, providing supports the authors say are "non-existent in most inquiry-based learning environments."
requirements: Handheld augmented reality game structures that position players as investigators developing and defending explanations
constraints: The authors note that time constraints alone might disqualify the game from being considered authentic in any meaningful respect
target_learners: middle school and similar-aged students in environmental science
examples: In Mad City Mystery, players investigated an environmental science mystery, developing narrative accounts of phenomena such as mercury contamination

article_title: Incidental vocabulary learning in a natural reading context: an eye-tracking study
citation: Aline Godfroid, Jieun Ahn, Ina Choi, Laura Ballard, Yaqiong Cui, Suzanne Johnston, Shinhye Lee, Abdhi Sarkar and Hyung-Jo Yoon (2017). Incidental vocabulary learning in a natural reading context: an eye-tracking study. Bilingualism: Language and Cognition, Volume 21, Issue 3. https://doi.org/10.1017/S1366728917000219
title: Post-reading comprehension test and three surprise vocabulary tests
description: After the reading sessions, "participants received a comprehension test and three surprise vocabulary tests". The surprise tests measured the "multifaceted vocabulary knowledge" — including "form and meaning" — that readers acquired incidentally while reading the novel, allowing learning outcomes to be linked to the eye-movement record.
requirements: Administered after the reading task is complete, so scores reflect learning from the preceding reading
target_learning_goals: measurement of incidental vocabulary knowledge of form and meaning
examples: Participants received a comprehension test and three surprise vocabulary tests after reading five novel chapters

article_title: Complicating Access: Digital Inequality and Adult Learning in a Public Access Computing Space
citation: Smythe, S., & Breshears, S. (2017). Complicating Access: Digital Inequality And Adult Learning In A Public-Access Computing Space. The Canadian Journal for the Study of Adult Education, 29(1), 67-81. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1139334
title: Policy anthropology "studying through" approach tracing digital access from policy texts to the lives of those affected
description: The article adopts a policy anthropology approach (Wedel & Feldman, 2005) employing "studying through," in which policy analysis follows "the source of a policy—its discourses, prescriptions, and programs—through to those affected by the policies." It combines a wide lens of critical policy analysis with a finely grained ethnographic lens into actual use and experiences of digital access and learning, treating policy as an imaginary that imposes ideal types of the "normal" citizen.
requirements: A complementary spatial perspective bringing into focus both local lives and distant policy actors within the same frame.
constraints: The authors note a shorter-term ethnographic study could not trace wavering access over time, and policy analysis alone could not capture disconnections between imaginaries and actualities.
target_learners: Adult educators and policy makers seeking to understand digital inequality
target_learning_goals: Understanding how digital policies materialize in everyday adult learning experiences
examples: The study mapped federal, provincial, and municipal digital policy texts, then followed them into the Digital Café ethnography of Malek's access story.

article_title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness Is Associated with Selective Attention in Healthy Male High-School Students
citation: Wengaard E, Kristoffersen M, Harris A and Gundersen H (2017) Cardiorespiratory Fitness Is Associated with Selective Attention in Healthy Male High-School Students. Front. Hum. Neurosci. 11:330. https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2017.00330
title: Posner cue paradigm visual cognitive task with three stimuli categories for assessing selective attention and inhibitory control
description: The study used a pc-based visual cognitive task based on the Posner cue paradigm to assess reaction time, accuracy and inhibition. The task presented 336 target stimuli across three categories: "no cue", "valid cue" and "invalid cue", where 56 (17%) appeared without a cue, 224 (67%) in the same rectangle as the cue, and 56 (17%) in the opposite rectangle. Participants fixated on a crosshair and pressed keys to indicate which rectangle the target asterisk appeared in, instructed to ignore the cue stimulus.
requirements: Performed on a 13.3-inch laptop programmed with E-prime 2.0
Carried out in a quiet location without distractions, wearing hearing protectors
Oral instruction and a small practice run before the actual task
constraints: Task duration was 9 min and 20 s
The order of inter-stimuli interval, stimuli and cues was fixed for all participants
examples: Mean RT was 376 ± 31 ms for no cue, 293 ± 28 ms for valid cue and 353 ± 35 ms for invalid cue stimuli; error rates were 3.3%, 5.9% and 10.0% respectively

article_title: Reading enjoyment amongst non-leisure readers can affect achievement in secondary school
citation: Mol SE and Jolles J (2014) Reading enjoyment amongst non-leisure readers can affect achievement in secondary school. Front. Psychol. 5:1214. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01214
title: Positive spiral of reciprocal causation between leisure reading, skills, enjoyment, and achievement
description: The article organizes its predictions around a reciprocal-causation account in which leisure reading builds academic skills, which in turn sustain enjoyment and voluntary reading. The article states that "A positive spiral of reciprocal causation seems to explain that leisure readers increase skills that are important for their academic success, such as their vocabulary and reading comprehension." Better skilled readers are described as more likely to enjoy reading, continue voluntarily, and raise school performance, while non-leisure readers are placed at highest risk of poor achievement. The study uses this model to motivate examining enjoyment and imagery among non-leisure readers in both educational tracks.
requirements: Applies to voluntary leisure reading of books; the article notes it is unknown whether other text types (newspapers, blogs, informative websites) feed the same spiral.
constraints: The article treats the spiral as an explanatory model, not a tested causal path; its own study is correlational.
target_learners: Secondary school students in early adolescence (12- to 13-year-old seventh graders)
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension, vocabulary, and academic achievement in language-based school subjects
examples: The survey of 1,071 Dutch seventh graders tested the model's prediction that non-leisure readers who enjoy reading achieve more, confirming it in most subgroups.

article_title: A decade of CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl. (2015). A decade of CSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-015-9222-2
title: Group-level post-cognitive paradigm of CSCL: cognition and knowledge building occur at dialogical, small-group and community levels beyond the individual mind
description: The editorial describes the founding theoretical shift of CSCL: transcending cognitive science by extending the unit of cognition beyond individual mental representations to structures of interaction. The author writes that it was time to extend "the unit of cognition beyond the boundaries of the individual mind" and that post-cognitive theories "began to postulate structures and practices at the group level." This paradigm, drawing on distributed cognition, activity theory and conversation analysis, dominates CSCL theory and frames collaborative learning as meaning negotiation and dialogical interaction rather than individual knowledge transfer.
requirements: Research and technology must treat small-group interaction, not individual cognition, as the primary unit of analysis
constraints: The article notes the paradigm has been less influential in technology design and analysis methodology than in theory
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students engaged in collaborative learning
examples: The editorial cites the Virtual Math Teams Project as a concrete model of DBR exploring CSCL technology, pedagogy, curriculum, methodology and theory within an integrated post-cognitive approach

article_title: Divisive or facilitative: The two faces of technology in CSCL
citation: Carolyn P. Rosé, Sten Ludvigsen, Nancy Law, Ulrike Cress & Gerry Stahl. (2017). Divisive or facilitative: The two faces of technology in CSCL. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 12:215–220. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-017-9265-7
title: Positioning theory as a lens for power relationships and authority during collaboration
description: Positioning theory, attributed to Davies and Harré, treats the rhetorical choices made by speakers as negotiating a place within a conceptual space relative to one another. The editors describe it as a lens for studying power relationships and authority over knowledge in collaboration, with dimensions including emotional closeness, power, and status. Unlike roles, positioning can change over an extended interaction, which makes status differences achievements in interaction.
requirements: An extended interaction to observe, since shifts in positioning unfold from time to time and are consequential for interaction analysis
constraints: Contrasted with the concept of roles, which are more static; positioning is dynamic rather than fixed
target_learners: secondary school students in collaborative pairs
target_learning_goals: negotiating power and status during peer collaboration around shared technology
examples: The editorial reports that two case-study dyads were examined as positioning was negotiated over time, both individually and in comparison to one another

article_title: CSCL artifacts
citation: G. Stahl & S. Ludvigsen & N. Law & U. Cress. (2014). CSCL artifacts. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning, 9, 237–245. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9200-0
title: Post-cognitive CSCL approach: dialectical, interactional and dynamic analysis of group meaning making
description: The editorial summarizes the CSCL paradigm as a post-cognitive approach 'dialectical (the problem and technological artifacts that mediate the group interaction must be seen to be enacted by that interaction), interactional (group-cognitive phenomena should not be reduced to individual mental structures)'. It is 'dynamic (there should be a concern with developmental processes at multiple levels)'. Learning is treated as essentially intersubjective and interactional, studied at the group unit of analysis rather than through individual pre/post outcomes.
requirements: Analysis must investigate dynamic developmental processes through which individual, small-group and community cognitive practices emerge
constraints: Group-cognitive phenomena are not to be reduced to individual mental structures
target_learners: student dyads and small groups in CSCL settings
target_learning_goals: group-level meaning making and collaborative knowledge construction
examples: The two empirical papers in the issue are described as adopting and advancing this dialectical, interactional and dynamic paradigm

article_title: Teachers rehumanizing mathematics for students with disabilities; the role of empathy
citation: Rachel Lambert, Kara Imm. (2026). Teachers rehumanizing mathematics for students with disabilities; the role of empathy. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09753-4
title: Political/relational model of disability as the framing for rehumanizing mathematics professional development
description: The study situated disability in a political/relational model influenced by feminist and queer studies, in place of the traditional medical model focused on diagnosing and fixing individual deficits. This model "centers disability as an embodied experience that intersects with social conditions," defining disability in relation to shifting standards of normalcy and highlighting the curative imaginary. The professional development used this framing, alongside the disability rights movement and critical disability texts, to prompt educators to reassess deficit views of disabled mathematics learners.
requirements: Educators encounter political perspectives on disability rights and activism, not only individual-deficit framings
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptual framing for the PD and analysis, not a tested instructional manipulation
target_learners: Mathematics and special educators teaching students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: Rethinking ideas about disability; disrupting deficit thinking; analyzing oppressive systems
examples: Among the 10 survey participants who referenced political struggles related to disability, 9 specifically mentioned the Disability Rights Movement and/or the documentary Crip Camp.

article_title: Using DNA to Predict Education: a Meta-analytic Review
citation: Wilding, K., Wright, M., & von Stumm, S. (2024). Using DNA to Predict Education: a Meta-analytic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09928-4
title: Polygenic scores as probabilistic, non-causal predictors of educational outcomes
description: Polygenic scores are person-specific aggregates of inherited DNA differences, computed by aggregating SNPs identified in GWAS weighted by their effect size. The article defines them as indexing "person-specific estimates of genetic propensities for a given target phenotype", while also capturing environmental variances due to gene-environment correlations, assortative mating, and population stratification. They are stable across the lifespan, unaffected by self-report biases, normally distributed, and modeled as continuous variables. Crucially, they are probabilistic rather than deterministic or causal predictors of phenotypic outcomes.
requirements: Genotype data in independent samples and GWAS summary statistics identifying SNPs associated with the target phenotype
constraints: They are probabilistic rather than deterministic or causal predictors of phenotypic outcomes, and they also capture environmental influences
Polygenic scores based on GWAS in European ancestry populations have limited prediction in populations of other ancestries
target_learners: children and adolescents in education systems whose learning differences may be predicted from DNA
target_learning_goals: prediction of individual differences in educational attainment and achievement to inform personalized learning and early intervention
examples: The article describes how GWAS summary statistics enable computing polygenic scores in independent samples by aggregating SNPs weighted by their effect size, and how scores from the Lee et al. (2018) GWAS were used across the 18 retained studies.

article_title: Evermore Wellbeing for Teens: A Scoping Review of Stand-alone and Brief Positive Psychology Interventions for Potential Use in Educational Settings
citation: Lucciarini, E., Carr, A., Bressoud, N., Boniwell, I., Audrin, C., Gay, P., & Burel, N. (2025). Evermore Wellbeing for Teens: A Scoping Review of Stand-alone and Brief Positive Psychology Interventions for Potential Use in Educational Settings. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10033-3
title: PoETA: a toolbox approach of short, stand-alone, flexible positive psychology interventions for classroom integration
description: PoETA (Lucciarini & Boniwell, 2023) is a framework for integrating wellbeing practices into schools through a curated toolbox of brief interventions. The article states that "The PoETA aims at providing short (5 to 10 min), stand-alone, explicit, and flexible interventions that require minimal or no specialised training." It complements rather than replaces CASEL and SAFE, targeting implementation barriers of time, training, and curricular flexibility, and lets teachers and students select activities. The authors stress that effectiveness in real classrooms still requires dedicated validation studies.

constraints: Pending further validation in real-world educational settings; substantial research is still needed to confirm its effectiveness
examples: The review screened Carr et al.'s (2023) mega-analysis and retained 64 interventions meeting PoETA's brevity, stand-alone, and evidence criteria

article_title: Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data
citation: Dumas, D., Goecke, B., Kagan, S., & Weiss, S. (2026). Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10110-7
title: Large-scale assessments reverse the individual-measurement logic: population distributions are modeled first and student scores generated from them
description: The article articulates an epistemic framework contrasting two measurement traditions. In the psychoeducational tradition, individual students' minds are 'upstream from all other patterns we observe', with population inferences extrapolated from reliable individual scores. Large-scale assessments reverse this: 'modeling population distributions as conditioned on student background variables first and then generating student test scores'. The framework organizes the paper's comparison of what each data type can validly support.
requirements: Analysts must understand which measurement tradition a dataset comes from before choosing analytic procedures
constraints: The framework applies to performance-assessment aspects of large-scale assessments; self-report questionnaires are less affected by planned missingness at the item level
target_learners: educational researchers and secondary analysts of assessment data
target_learning_goals: understanding valid inference from large-scale assessment data
examples: Table 1 of the article contrasts individual measures and large-scale assessments across dimensions such as construct coverage, score type, and level of valid inference

article_title: Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data
citation: Dumas, D., Goecke, B., Kagan, S., & Weiss, S. (2026). Zooming Out On Education: Making Valid Psychological Inferences From Large-Scale Assessment Data. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10110-7
title: Make inferences from plausible values only at the population level, conditional on the assessment design
description: The article's central recommendation: with large-scale assessment data, 'inferences are only possible at the population-level—and then only when framed as conditional on the assessment design and assumptions—not at the level of individual students'. Findings can inform system-level policy decisions but not classroom-level instructional decisions about individual students.
requirements: Analyses must correctly incorporate the sampling design and the multiple-imputation logic for PVs before any population-level inference is valid
constraints: Reporting percentages of students above or below a threshold is invalid because a student having low PVs does not necessarily imply they even took the assessment in question
target_learners: educational psychologists and policy researchers using secondary assessment data
target_learning_goals: drawing valid inferences about population distributions of academic abilities
examples: It is valid to say a population average is higher or lower from one wave to the next or across countries, but not to extrapolate that a different percentage of students scored poorly

article_title: Towards a new, complexity science of learning and education
citation: Jörg, T., Davis, B. & Nickmans, G. (2007). Towards a new, complexity science of learning and education. Educational Research Review, 2(2), 145–156. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2007.09.002
title: Orient education toward possibility and potentiality rather than pre-specified ends
description: Under the complexity paradigm, the article recommends abandoning the desire to pre-determine outcomes and framing education in possibility-oriented rather than ends-oriented terms. As Morin is quoted, 'we should be realistic in a complex way, understanding the uncertainty of reality, knowing that the real holds invisible potential'. Learning trajectories are pictured as paths through multidimensional transitional spaces of possibility.
requirements: Recognition that the way things unfold is inherently unknowable and emerges through spontaneous self-organisation rather than advanced planning
constraints: The article acknowledges this raises unresolved ethical questions about which specialisations are chosen and who decides
target_learning_goals: development of expansive possibilities and potentialities of learning
examples: The article suggests policy-makers entrust schools, teacher groups, classroom collectives and individuals with meaningful decision-making responsibilities and opportunities to specialise, noting contemporary schools tend to minimise learner or classroom specialisation.

article_title: The Powerful Teacher: A Power Hypothesis for the Benefits of Learning-by-Teaching
citation: Sarah Shi Hui Wong, Stephen Lim. (2026). The Powerful Teacher: A Power Hypothesis for the Benefits of Learning-by-Teaching. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10097-1
title: Power hypothesis of learning-by-teaching
description: The article advances a novel mechanism account: "when taking on the role of a teacher and teaching others, students might experience a heightened sense of power that may be beneficial for their own learning." Power is defined as a psychological state of perceived capacity to influence others, distinct from social presence, autonomy, self-efficacy, and productive agency. Drawing on French and Raven's power bases, the account holds that the teacher role carries expectations of authoritative knowledge, and that power triggers approach orientation, energized cognition, and self-regulation that improve task performance.
requirements: The learner must take on the role of a teacher, which carries socially structured expectations of authoritative knowledge and responsibility for the audience's learning.
constraints: The account is presented as a hypothesis tested in non-interactive, written teaching with a fictitious peer audience; the article distinguishes power from social presence, which can manifest without interaction.
examples: Participants in the teaching condition wrote a verbatim teaching script as how they would orally deliver a lecture to their peers, and rated their sense of power during the intervention.
key_sources: Sarah Shi Hui Wong, Stephen Lim. (2026). The Powerful Teacher: A Power Hypothesis for the Benefits of Learning-by-Teaching. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10097-1

article_title: Possibility mindset: A theory of motivation under constraint, with neurodivergence as a revealing interpretive case
citation: Srinivasan, H. (2026). Possibility Mindset: A Theory of Motivation Under Constraint, with Neurodivergence as a Revealing Interpretive Case. Preprint (v1) posted to PsyArXiv on January 18, 2026. https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv
title: Possibility mindset: a context-specific appraisal of 'room to move' grounded in three belief dimensions
description: Possibility mindset is defined as a learner's integrated appraisal of perceived room to move within a specific learning context, grounded in three belief dimensions: self-change beliefs (can I develop in ways that matter here?), environment-change beliefs (will this setting adapt reliably in practice?), and pathway-flexibility beliefs (are there multiple legitimate routes to valued goals?). The article positions it within the attributional tradition, specifying how attributions about systems, rather than solely about the self, shape motivational decisions under enduring constraint. It is offered as complementary to growth mindset, not a replacement for it.
requirements: Measurement of beliefs about environments and pathways alongside self-beliefs, so that misalignment profiles are not misread as motivational failure
constraints: Applies to contexts where effort alone cannot reliably secure access; the article states it is not a need-based or autonomy-based theory but an appraisal of feasibility
target_learners: Disabled and neurodivergent learners, including autistic learners
Learners in educational contexts where effort alone cannot reliably remove barriers
examples: The article defines the construct via three questions: 'Can I change? Will the setting change? Are there legitimate routes?'

description: The article proposes using the education polygenic score (education-PGS), a composite of genetic variants associated with completing more years of school, as a "molecular tracer" of students through the high school math pipeline. target_learning_goals: Understanding how students flow through the secondary school math pipeline and how school context shapes advanced mathematics coursetaking

citation: Jia, Y., Spagnolo, A. B., Barrett, N., Murphy, A. A., Basto, P. M., Rothpletz-Puglia, P., & Luther, S. (2025). Validation of a peer observation and evaluation tool for online teaching in the U.S. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10428-z
title: Peer Observation and Evaluation Tool-Online (POET-O)
description: The POET-O is a peer observation and evaluation instrument for single online lessons, created by "modifying and adapting the POET (Trujillo et al., 2008) by adding selected items from the Quality Matters rubric." The final instrument has 32 items across five sections: Presentation and Activities (7 items), Use of Technology (5), ADA Compliance/Accessibility (4), Assessment (3), and Instructor (13), each rated on a 4-point scale from "Not Present" to "Accomplished Well" with a "Not Applicable" option. The complete tool includes pre-observation, observation, general reviewer comments, post-observation, and faculty reflection and action plan sections.
requirements: Requires standardized training and/or debriefing of faculty reviewers to ensure reliable and consistent assessment
Requires lesson submitters to provide course materials, syllabus, and assessment items for review
constraints: Validated only for online synchronous and asynchronous lessons; the authors state it "should be further evaluated" for in-person lab/practice-based lessons
Does not include peer assessment of the use of learning theory or teaching philosophy

article_title: Precision diagnosis in virtual learning contexts: a predict-observe-explain-diagnose-based approach to scientific inquiry
citation: Kuan‑Fu Chen, Gwo‑Jen Hwang, Mei‑Rong Alice Chen. (2025). Precision diagnosis in virtual learning contexts: a predict‑observe‑explain‑diagnose‑based approach to scientific inquiry. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10527-5
title: POED strategy: extending POEE with a two-tier diagnostic test phase that diagnoses misconceptions and guides knowledge reconstruction
description: The POED strategy extends the Predict-Observe-Explain-Evaluate (POEE) strategy by replacing the evaluation phase with a two-tier test-based diagnosis phase. The article states that "a two-tier test-based learning diagnosis strategy was adopted to replace the evaluation in POEE to diagnose learners' misconceptions and guide them to construct correct knowledge and concepts". In the implemented VR system, students progress through prediction, observation, explanation, and evaluation scenes, then take a two-tier test whose first tier verifies factual knowledge and second tier requires conceptual justification; incorrect answers prompt a choice between retrying or reading supplementary learning materials, and progression is contingent on passing both tiers.
requirements: A two-tier test database with teacher-designed diagnostic questions and supplementary learning materials, plus a learning process database recording student behavior
constraints: The article notes the two-tier test questions were limited to multiple-choice questions only, which it says cannot diagnose some misconceptions
target_learners: eighth-grade junior high school natural science students
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of factors affecting chemical reaction rate
diagnosis and correction of science misconceptions
examples: The system was implemented with UPTALENT SVVR for the natural science course topic of factors influencing the chemical reaction rate, with 10 two-tier diagnostic questions developed by teachers with 10 years of experience

description: A spherical video-based virtual reality (SVVR) learning system implemented with UPTALENT for a junior high school natural science course. article_title: The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities
citation: Lina Markauskaite, Lucila Carvalho, Tim Fawns. (2023). The role of teachers in a sustainable university: from digital competencies to postdigital capabilities. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10199-z
title: Postdigital teaching capabilities: an ecological, distributed and relational framework
description: The article proposes that teaching capabilities in a postdigital university are "distributed and relational", extending across an activity system that includes other people, culture, environment and the embodied self. It draws on theories of cognition that see human capabilities as "extended, enacted, embedded, enculturated and embodied", arguing that what teachers know cannot be separated from their feelings, material and digital environments, and social others. The framework situates capabilities at macro (global), meso (local practices) and micro (daily activities) levels of the educational ecosystem.
requirements: Conceptualisations must describe capabilities that extend across an activity system rather than properties inherent in an individual
constraints: The article presents this as a conceptual proposal offered as an entry point, not an empirically validated model
target_learning_goals: teaching with digital technologies in sustainable, future-oriented universities
examples: The article grounds the framework in ecopedagogies, pedagogies of care and pedagogies of self-care as complementary postdigital pedagogies at macro, meso and micro levels

article_title: Accessibility and emotionality of online assessment feedback: Using emoticons to enhance student perceptions of marker competence and warmth
citation: Moffitt, RL; Padgett, C; Grieve, R. (2020). Accessibility and emotionality of online assessment feedback: Using emoticons to enhance student perceptions of marker competence and warmth. Computers and Education, 143. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2019.103654
title: Use positively valenced emoticons in written online assessment feedback to add warmth without sacrificing perceived quality or professionalism
description: The article concludes that instructors can use positively valenced emoticons to inject emotionality into written online assessment feedback. As the authors put it, instructors can use emoticons "to inject some fun, warmth, and emotionality in written online assessment feedback without sacrificing feedback quality or professional integrity." The recommendation rests on the experiment showing warmth and competence benefits for happy emoticons with null effects on quality and professionalism.
requirements: Feedback is written and delivered online in a higher education assessment context
constraints: Benefits were demonstrated for positively valenced emoticons; negatively valenced emoticons lowered perceived warmth and competence
Perceived competence advantage was reported specifically for 3 happy face emoticons
target_learning_goals: student perceptions of feedback accessibility, emotionality, and marker warmth and competence
examples: Undergraduates (N = 241) read a faux essay with written feedback identical except for emoticon frequency (none, 1, 3, or 6) and valence (happy, sad, or confused) in a between-groups experiment

article_title: The effect of a computer-based cartooning tool on children’s cartoons and written stories
citation: M. Madden, P.W.H. Chung, C.W. Dawson. (2007). The Effect of a Computer-Based Cartooning Tool On Children's Cartoons and Written Stories. Loughborough University Institutional Repository. http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/2.5/
title: Computer-based cartooning tool with posable characters, camera controls and visual storytelling prompts
description: The tool lets users build sequences of still shots from backgrounds, clipart and character artwork; characters can be "'posed' via one interaction mode which allows limbs in a skeleton to be dragged with the mouse, and 'warped' via another interaction mode which allows simple manipulation of vector control points". It provides camera point-of-view controls, a sequence bar with undo/redo and a full-screen slide show, and optional "visual storytelling prompts" offering ideas, character and camera help per story stage. No typing interface for captions is provided, deliberately emphasising purely visual communication.
requirements: Pre-supplied character artwork created by the investigator, since the character-creation framework was judged unsuitable for novice users
An ICT suite with shared computers, since storywriting was done on paper in class
constraints: The current version probably made depicting emotion harder than on paper
No side views of characters were provided, making some poses such as bowing difficult
The visual storytelling prompts were too low-key and rarely accessed
examples: Used in two sub-studies to prepare retellings of The Ramayana and The Visitor before written versions were collected

article_title: Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks
citation: Jones, I. (2008). Storyboarding: A method for bootstrapping the design of computer-based educational tasks. https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/
title: PowerPoint storyboarding tool and procedures
description: The tool used was Microsoft PowerPoint, chosen because it was already installed and easy to use. Copy and paste tools allowed new slides to be cloned with minor stepwise adjustments, and the "click to add notes" facility allowed slides to be annotated and date-stamped to build a time-line of evolving ideas. Files were shared with a colleague who added date-stamped comments as feedback.
requirements: Copy and paste tools for cloning slides
Manual dating and formatting of comments, since PowerPoint lacks a Reviewing mode
constraints: PowerPoint does not offer a Reviewing mode and comments had to be manually dated and formatted
Drawing tools are constrained to basic shapes and text

article_title: Simulation in podiatry teaching and learning: A scoping review.
citation: Anning Naomi, Tehan Peta. (2024). Simulation in podiatry teaching and learning: A scoping review. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1002/jfa2.70020
title: Six-theme taxonomy of simulation purposes in podiatry education
description: The review organizes the podiatry simulation literature by the purpose of the simulation intervention, grouping studies into six themes: "skill improvement, communication and professionalism, clinical competencies and patient safety, educational enhancement, and anatomy and histology education". Content analysis of included studies was charted into tables by these purposes, alongside study design, participants, simulation modality, and main findings, to draw links between purpose, modality, and findings.
requirements: Content analysis of included studies charted by purpose of simulation intervention, study design, participants, modality, and main findings
constraints: Further quantitative synthesis was not possible due to the diverse scope of included data
examples: Table 1 charts each included study under one of the six purpose categories, from anatomic wound models for diabetic foot ulcers to virtual microscopes for histology

article_title: A Scoping Review of Interprofessional Simulation-Based Team Training Programs.
citation: Bochatay N, Ju M, O'Brien BC, van Schaik SM. (2025). A Scoping Review of Interprofessional Simulation-Based Team Training Programs. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000792
title: Power and intergroup relations theories as a lens for redesigning ISBTT
description: The review proposes that ISBTT programs implicitly rely on contact theory, whose prerequisite of equal status is rarely met in hierarchical healthcare teams. It argues that engaging with "theoretical concepts related to power and intergroup relations" — including French and Raven's social bases of power and Strauss's negotiated order perspective — can help programs explicitly address barriers to collaboration, inform debriefing content, and explain tensions such as inexperienced physician trainees leading experienced nurses.
requirements: Programs must engage with theoretical and conceptual frameworks developed to understand power and intergroup relations, as the review recommends
constraints: The review notes that while power dynamics are unlikely to change through education programs alone, programs can equip participants to navigate them
target_learners: Health professionals from at least 2 professions participating in simulation-based team training
target_learning_goals: Navigating power discrepancies and hierarchies in interprofessional teams
Managing conflict and building social capital in collaborative practice
examples: The review describes how the negotiated order perspective explains tensions when inexperienced physician trainees act as team leaders giving instructions to experienced nurses

article_title: Longitudinal Associations Between Childhood Obesity and Academic Achievement: Systematic Review with Focus Group Data.
citation: Martin A, Booth JN, McGeown S, Niven A, Sproule J, Saunders DH, Reilly JJ. (2017). Longitudinal Associations Between Childhood Obesity and Academic Achievement: Systematic Review with Focus Group Data. Current Obesity Reports, 6(3), 297–313. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13679-017-0272-9
title: Physical Education should be a positive, supportive experience for children and adolescents with obesity
description: The review concludes that PE environments can be sites of weight-related teasing and perceived teacher bias for adolescents with obesity, and recommends that "Physical Education should be a positive experience for children and adolescents with obesity". This includes PE teachers understanding motivation processes and delivering educational experiences that teach the values and benefits of physical activity for sustained participation. The principle addresses the psychosocial barriers that may undermine both wellbeing and engagement in physical activity among learners with obesity.
requirements: PE teachers should understand the complexity of motivation processes to deliver positive PE experiences for adolescents with obesity
constraints: Evidence for teacher bias towards obese children is empirically inconsistent, per the review
examples: Focus group participants reported feeling ignored and excluded from activities by PE teachers, and classroom teachers were perceived as non-judgmental towards increased body weight

article_title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of selected motor learning principles in physiotherapy and medical education.
citation: Sattelmayer Martin, Elsig Simone, Hilfiker Roger, Baer Gillian. (2016). A systematic review and meta-analysis of selected motor learning principles in physiotherapy and medical education. BMC Medical Education, 16, 15. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0538-z
title: Learning-versus-performance test framework: post-acquisition, retention, and transfer tests measure different aspects of motor learning
description: The review organises outcome measurement for procedural skill learning into three test types. Post-acquisition tests measure performance immediately after intervention but "should not be associated with a relatively permanent change associated with learning". Retention tests insert a rest period so non-permanent effects are eliminated, and transfer tests assess adapting the skill to a different situation. The review uses this framework to interpret all four motor learning principle comparisons.
requirements: Learning must be inferred from relatively permanent improvement in performance, requiring delayed measurement rather than immediate post-testing
constraints: Post-acquisition tests provide only limited evidence of learning because observed changes may reflect transient performance effects
target_learners: medical and physiotherapy students and residents learning procedural skills
target_learning_goals: acquisition and retention of procedural (motor) skills
examples: The review advocates delayed retention and transfer tests: educators should be aware it is not safe to make inferences about learning with post-acquisition tests

article_title: Process oriented guided inquiry learning (POGIL®) marginally effects student achievement measures but substantially increases the odds of passing a course.
citation: Walker L, Warfa A-R M. (2017). Process oriented guided inquiry learning (POGIL®) marginally effects student achievement measures but substantially increases the odds of passing a course. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0186203
title: POGIL: a guided-inquiry pedagogy coupling process skills to content learning through a three-phase learning cycle
description: POGIL is a pedagogy, rooted in chemistry but used across disciplines, that "provides opportunities for improving process skills during content learning through guided-inquiry activities". Its materials use a learning cycle of three phases: exploration of a model, concept invention, and application. Students take individual roles within small groups (manager, reporter, skeptic) to establish positive interdependence, and well-designed activities target one or two of seven process skills: communication, teamwork, management, information processing, critical thinking, problem solving, and self-assessment.
requirements: Well-designed POGIL activities with one or two process skill targets
Students taking up individual roles within small group learning communities
constraints: The meta-analyzed studies could not confirm whether experimental groups strictly used POGIL activities or their frequency of use; some analyzed studies likely used activities not endorsed by The POGIL Project
target_learning_goals: transferable process skills such as collaboration, critical thinking, and problem solving
examples: The meta-analysis synthesized 21 studies comparing POGIL classrooms to standard lecture conditions, most with identical content coverage apart from the POGIL intervention

article_title: Effects of Project-Based Learning Strategy on Self-Directed Learning Skills of Educational Technology Students
citation: Bagheri, M., Wan Ali, W. Z., Abdullah, M. C. B., & Daud, S. M. (2013). Effects of Project-based Learning Strategy on Self-directed Learning Skills of Educational Technology Students. Contemporary Educational Technology, 4(1), 15-29. https://cedtech.net
title: Project-based learning organized around eight principles with a five-phase project procedure
description: The article describes PoBL as implemented through eight principles: "the organization of learning around real world problems; student centered instruction; collaboration; teacher as facilitator; authenticity through the use of authentic materials and audiences; formative assessment; reflection; and the production of authentic artifacts". The experimental group worked through five phases — organizing groups, stating subjects, designing the project, applying it, presenting, and evaluating — over two projects, each completed in six weeks, covering all course concepts.
requirements: Students assigned to mixed-ability groups with explained group-working rules
Projects based on course concepts, covering systematic investigation of an educational problem and application of instructional design procedures
constraints: Each project required six weeks of group work, with substantial time spent out of class
examples: In the experimental group, students in five groups of 7-8 designed and applied two projects in real settings such as a high school in Arak city and the instructional technology department of Arak University, producing instructional software, weblogs, and presentations.

article_title: The Effect of Portfolio Assessment on Learning Idioms in Writing
citation: Abdorreza Tahriri, Masoud Khalili Sabet, Afrouz Aeineh. (2014). The Effect of Portfolio Assessment on Learning Idioms in Writing. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 2(2). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.2n.2p.53
title: Portfolio assessment procedure combining self-assessment, peer assessment, teacher feedback, and revision of writing samples
description: In this study, portfolio assessment was operationalized as an alternative assessment routine in which the experimental group kept their idiom-using writing in a portfolio: "The teacher commented on their writing" and a classmate also assessed it, after which students reflected on and revised their work and placed the revised version in the portfolio. The control group instead handed writing to the teacher solely to be rated. The routine ran across 10 sessions with five idioms taught per session.
requirements: Learners produce writing samples using target idioms that can be collected and revised in the portfolio
Teacher provides feedback and comments, and peers assess each other's writing
constraints: Studied with 30 upper-intermediate EFL learners aged 18-32 in a language institute in Rasht, Iran, over 10 sessions
target_learning_goals: knowledge and use of English idioms in writing
examples: The experimental group kept writing in the portfolio, received teacher comments and peer assessment, reflected, revised, and filed the revised version; the control group's writing was only rated by the teacher
