article_title: The Effect of Portfolio Assessment on Learning Idioms in Writing
citation: Abdorreza Tahriri, Masoud Khalili Sabet, Afrouz Aeineh. (2014). The Effect of Portfolio Assessment on Learning Idioms in Writing. International Journal of Education & Literacy Studies, 2(2). http://dx.doi.org/10.7575/aiac.ijels.v.2n.2p.53
title: Portfolio as authentic assessment with learner choice, feedback-driven revision, reflection, evidence of mastery, and multi-form artifacts
description: The article enumerates five characteristics of portfolio as an assessment and learning tool: "The learner can decide what to put in the portfolio"; learners can revise materials after receiving teacher or peer feedback; assessing and reflecting on portfolio work makes learners aware of their progress; there is evidence of mastery of knowledge; and artifacts can take many forms such as written work, audio recording, or video recording. The article classifies portfolio as a kind of authentic assessment because it includes samples of actual student performance elicited under normal classroom conditions.
requirements: Learner control over portfolio contents
Feedback and comments from teacher or peers enabling revision
Learner assessment and reflection on the work in the portfolio
constraints: The article notes not all performance assessments are authentic; portfolio is a special case of performance assessment done in an authentic classroom context
target_learning_goals: learner awareness of progress and personal development
examples: In the study, learners decided to include their idiom-using writing samples, revised them after teacher and peer comments, and archived them to see improvement over time

article_title: The Effects of Diagrams and Questioning-While-Reading on Learning from a Statistics Lesson
citation: Clinton, V., Alibali, M. W., & Nathan, M. J. (2013). The effects of diagrams and questioning-while-reading on learning from a statistics lesson. In Martinez, M. & Castro Superfine, A. (Eds.), Proceedings of the 35th annual meeting of the North American Chapter of the International Group for the Psychology of Mathematics Education. Chicago, IL: University of Illinois at Chicago.
title: Posterior probability lesson with natural frequencies, optional diagrams, and embedded questions or elaborative interrogations
description: A paper-and-pencil statistics lesson adapted from Heuer (1999) with materials from Sedlmeier and Gigerenzer's (2001) experiments, presenting "two examples of scenarios in which base rate and specificity probabilities were presented, and then the posterior probability was calculated using natural frequencies." Diagram conditions varied whether diagram information was also in the text; questioning conditions placed one question after approximately every paragraph. The lesson was evaluated in a randomized experiment with 245 undergraduates.
requirements: All lessons began with a reminder that participants would answer questions based on the lesson; control participants were instructed to read the lesson twice.
constraints: Posttest and pretest problems were presented as text only, with no visuals.
target_learning_goals: calculating posterior probability from base rate and specificity information
examples: Embedded questions were simple with explicitly stated answers (e.g., "How many fighter jets identified as Vietnamese are actually Cambodian?"); elaborative interrogations were complex "how" and "why" questions with answers implicit in the text.

article_title: Polyrhythmic Tapping: Examining the Effectiveness of the Strategy of Organizing Rhythmic Structures through Synthesis
citation: Hamit Yokus, Tuba Yokus. (2015). Polyrhythmic Tapping: Examining the Effectiveness of the Strategy of Organizing Rhythmic Structures through Synthesis. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice. https://doi.org/10.12738/estp.2015.1.1917
title: Polyrhythmic Tapping Test
description: A researcher-developed measuring instrument aiming "to quantify competency in the performance of 3:2, 4:3, 8:3, 5:4 and 3:5 polyrhythmic structures." It contains 87 polyrhythmic structures across 4 sub-dimensions, scored 1 point per structure (maximum 87, minimum 0), with target structures contrasted against 1:1, 2:1 and 3:1 structures. Metronome tempo is 50 for the first three sub-dimensions and 40 for the fourth. Validity and reliability were checked with 43 students; KR-20 coefficients were .71, .81, .96 and .94 per sub-dimension and .92 overall.
requirements: Administration with a metronome, individual performance tapping with a pencil, and scoring by three specialists with video recording to resolve ambiguous situations
constraints: The test was validated with first- and second-year students (N = 43) at a single university's music education program
target_learning_goals: polyrhythmic tapping competency for 3:2, 4:3, 8:3, 5:4 and 3:5 structures
examples: Used as pre-test and post-test for both groups; each student performed the structures with left and right hand accompanied by the metronome without stopping

citation: Kousar Perveen. (2010). Effect Of The Problem-Solving Approach On Academic Achievement Of Students In Mathematics At The Secondary Level. Contemporary Issues In Education Research, 3(3).
title: Polya's four-step heuristic problem-solving framework
description: The article uses Polya's framework, in which problem-solving is "the process used to solve a problem that does not have an obvious solution" and teaching it means teaching "strategies, or heuristics". The four-step process is: 1) understand the problem, 2) devise a plan, 3) carry out the plan, and 4) look back. The experimental group's lesson plans were built on these heuristic steps together with Shireen (2006) guidelines.
requirements: Instruction must be organized as a sequence of heuristic steps applied to problems, per the Polya (1945) guidelines used to build the lesson plans
constraints: In this study the heuristics had to be preceded by exposition of facts, rules, formulas and procedures before students could use them
examples: The experimental group was taught using a series of lesson plans put together with the help of Shireen (2006) and Polya (1945) guidelines over six consecutive weeks

article_title: Effectiveness of Game and Poem Enhanced Instructional Strategies and Verbal Ability on Students' Interest in Mathematics Learning
citation: Frederick-Jonah, T. M. & Igbojinwaekwu, P. C. (2015). Effectiveness of Game and Poem Enhanced Instructional Strategies and Verbal Ability on Students’ Interest in Mathematics Learning. Journal of Research in Education, 25(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?q=Journal+of+Research+in+Education+Volume+25+Number+2
title: Use poems and games in primary mathematics instruction to enhance students’ interest
description: The article recommends that mathematics instruction at the primary level replace lecture-dominated teaching with poem- and game-enhanced activities, because these produced higher interest than the modified lecture strategy in its study. It states that "Mathematics teachers should give special attention to the use of poems and games to enhance students’ interest in mathematics." Poem activities involve reading, writing, and role-playing mathematical poems; games involve rule-governed, goal-directed play with mathematical structure.
requirements: Teachers need training in the poem- and game-enhanced instructional guides before use, as the study trained teachers for one week
constraints: Evidence comes from a two-week quasi-experiment on the concept of multiplication with primary 6 students in Bayelsa State, Nigeria

description: The article frames portfolio assessment as an alternative to one-shot traditional testing that aligns with the shift from product to process writing. The greater curvature simulates the uterus for incision and repair practice, with a scrubbing sponge inside to simulate uterine morphology, while a 3 cm incision in the pyloric region simulates a lacerated cervix for suturing practice. The total cost of the model is ￥41, using materials from the nearby market plus standard surgical instruments.
requirements: Fresh porcine stomach from a nearby market
Surgical instruments including ring forceps, needle holder, stitch scissors, Allis clamp, scalpel and coated Vicryl 2-0
Pre-processing of the stomach to remove grease and gastric acid before training
constraints: The hemorrhage cannot be simulated
The porcine stomach could not be kept long, especially in summer, and the smell of fresh porcine stomach might be troublesome
In countries where porcine or any animal stomachs are not readily available, the application of the simulation model is limited
target_learning_goals: Uterus incision and repair of cesarean section
examples: Used in OB/GYN surgical skills courses with a towel uterus model as a control; ring forceps inspection of the pyloric/cardia region simulates cervix inspection and two-layer running sutures simulate uterine repair
key_sources: Huang Yue, Jia Jin, Zhan Jun, Li Bo, Gu Qiong, Li Zhengyu. (2024). Porcine stomach surgical simulation model for cesarean section and cervical laceration suturing. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05936-8

article_title: Creation and validation of a high-fidelity simulation scenario for suicide postvention.
citation: Pedrollo Laysa Fernanda Silva; Silva Aline Conceição; Zanetti Ana Carolina Guidorizzi; Vedana Kelly Graziani Giacchero (2022). Creation and validation of a high-fidelity simulation scenario for suicide postvention. Revista Latino-Americana de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/1518-8345.6034.3699
title: Postvention framework: initial support actions for suicide bereaved people operationalized as welcoming, health care and organization monitoring
description: The article defines postvention as "a wide set of actions and strategies carried out after a death due to suicide with the survivors". The scenario turns this into three learning objectives — "welcoming, health care and organization monitoring" — and ten observable behaviors assessed by OSCE checklist, including enabling "conversation and listening spaces for bereaved people to recognize and express their feelings, experiences and needs, at their own pace and time".
requirements: Objectives and behaviors must be grounded in technical-scientific recommendations and current literature on suicide bereavement and postvention.
constraints: The article notes postvention approaches are "rarely portrayed in the scientific literature", which reinforces the stigma towards the theme and the difficulties approaching suicide.
target_learners: Health professionals in Primary Health Care
target_learning_goals: Initial support to suicide bereaved people: welcoming, health care and organization monitoring
examples: OSCE item 6 asks participants to "Evaluate the presence of suicidal and/or imitative behaviors in the bereaved".

citation: Zalewska Katarzyna, Zarzycka Danuta. (2022). International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph192214688
title: Polish adaptation of the Educational Practices Questionnaire (EPQ) with EPQ-PO and EPQ-IO sections
description: The Polish EPQ is a 16-item questionnaire measuring educational techniques used during high-fidelity simulation. As printed, the scale "consists of sixteen questions divided into the following subscales: Active Learning (items 1–10), Collaboration (items 11 and 12), Diverse Learning Methods (items 13 and 14), and High Expectations (items 15 and 16)". It has two parts: EPQ-PO on the presence of practices during classes and EPQ-IO on their importance to students. It was adapted via a six-stage WHO translation schema and validated with 361 nursing students.
requirements: Use of the tool required non-commercial use consent obtained according to National League for Nursing instructions for surveys and research instruments
constraints: Validated with second- and third-year undergraduate nursing students in Poland; master's students were excluded to ensure comparability of results
target_learning_goals: assessment of educational best practices in simulation
feedback to educators on teaching quality
examples: Students completed the paper version in about five minutes, without third parties present, after completing high-fidelity simulation classes

article_title: Validation of the portable virtual reality training system for robotic surgery (PoLaRS): a randomized controlled trial.
citation: Hardon Sem F., Kooijmans Anton, Horeman Roel, van der Elst Maarten, Bloemendaal Alexander L. A., Horeman Tim. (2022). Validation of the portable virtual reality training system for robotic surgery (PoLaRS): a randomized controlled trial. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-021-08906-z
title: PoLaRS portable virtual reality robotic surgery training system
description: PoLaRS (Portable Laparoscopic Robotic Surgery) is a prototype VR training system developed with Delft University of Technology to train fundamental robotic skills remotely. It consists of a console with two handles, each with seven degrees of movement, custom I/O circuitry, and VR software programmed in Unity run on a regular Windows laptop. The article states it "is designed to train fundamental robotic skills on a remote basis at an affordable cost of less than 25 k Euro per system", and it can be installed on a table top at any height for use from sitting or standing positions.
requirements: Requires a regular Windows laptop to run the Unity-based VR software and a table top surface for installation
constraints: Collision detection applies a 3-s cool-down period in a 10 mm radius, so longer collisions cause multiple collision counts compared to the dVSS
In this study all subjects used the PoLaRS system in a standing position, unlike the da Vinci system
target_learners: hospitals in less wealthy parts of the world
target_learning_goals: fundamental robotic surgical skills such as bimanual instrument handling and depth perception
examples: Test-group participants sorted marbles by color with left and right hands and passed marbles through circular cut-outs in walls on the PoLaRS prototype

title: Portuguese Law no. 60/2009 establishing mandatory school-based sexuality education with a teacher-coordinator
description: Law no. 60/2009 established the regime for sexuality education in Portuguese school settings, making it "mandatory in the educational projects of school clusters and non-clustered schools", with workload adapted to each educational level and distributed across the school year, under a psychosocial or biopsychosocial model. The review notes it established the figure of the teacher-coordinator responsible for introducing, supervising, and implementing sexuality education, and purposes including equality, protection against sexual abuse, and elimination of sexual discrimination. requirements: A teacher-coordinator appointed by each school responsible for implementation
A minimum number of hours of sexuality education in each grade

article_title: Exploring pooled analysis of pretested items to monitor the performance of medical students exposed to different curriculum designs.
citation: Hamamoto Filho PT, Lourenção PLTA, Abbade JF, Cecílio-Fernandes D, Caramori JT, Bicudo AM. (2021). Exploring pooled analysis of pretested items to monitor the performance of medical students exposed to different curriculum designs. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0257293
title: Pooled analysis of pretested items as a benchmark-assessment comparison method
description: A statistical method that compares cohorts on the same pretested assessment items by calculating per-item odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals and performing fixed-effects meta-analyses per content area. The article positions it against existing approaches, noting that "mean scores may not allow for reliable comparisons between scores on different exams because exams may have different levels of difficulty" and that cumulative deviation requires longitudinal appraisal. It provides item-level information on specific knowledge gaps beyond group-level comparisons.
requirements: Requires a benchmark assessment that re-uses pretested items so that different cohorts encounter the same items
Requires items divided into content areas for pooling
constraints: Cannot reduce the limitation of the low reliability of single measures
The article notes it is not expected to completely replace other tools, but to complement them
target_learning_goals: monitoring knowledge performance across curriculum designs
examples: The 2019 Interinstitutional Progress Test was built from items pretested between 2013 and 2018, allowing comparison of 63 items across six content areas between the 2019 cohort and earlier cohorts
key_sources: Hamamoto Filho PT, Lourenção PLTA, Abbade JF, Cecílio-Fernandes D, Caramori JT, Bicudo AM. (2021). article_title: Development and validation of a porcine organ model for training in essential laparoscopic surgical skills.
citation: Higuchi M, Abe T, Hotta K, et al. (2020). Development and validation of a porcine organ model for training in essential laparoscopic surgical skills. International Journal of Urology. https://doi.org/10.1111/iju.14315
title: Porcine cadaveric organ wet lab model for laparoscopic skills training
description: A wet laboratory training model using porcine cadaveric organs placed in a box trainer to teach core laparoscopic surgical skills outside the operating room. It comprises three tasks: tissue dissection around the aorta, tissue dissection and division of the renal artery, and renal parenchymal closure. The article states it was designed 'to develop a wet laboratory training model for learning core laparoscopic surgical skills and evaluating learners' competency level outside the operating room.'
requirements: Porcine cadaveric organs purchased from a commercial vendor
A box trainer (Endowork Pro II) with video system and 0° lens
Laparoscopic instruments including scissors, grasping forceps, clip applier, and needle holders
constraints: Lack of bleeding makes the training environment less stressful than live animal surgery
Fat tissue was rated as harder than in humans by participants
examples: Participants removed lymph nodes around the aorta and divided mesenteric vessels after applying Hem-o-lok clips
Participants passed a needle through kidney parenchyma completing three square single-throw knots using a slip-knot technique

article_title: How is self-regulated learning documented in e-portfolios of trainees? A content analysis.
citation: van der Gulden R, Heeneman S, Kramer AWM, Laan RFJM, Scherpbier-de Haan ND, Thoonen BPA. (2020). How is self-regulated learning documented in e-portfolios of trainees? A content analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02114-4
title: Portfolio-supported SRL process framework: self-assessment via reflection and feedback, goal-setting and planning, and monitoring
description: The article organises portfolio-relevant SRL around processes that the health professions education literature reports as supported by portfolios. "The health professions education literature generally reports the following SRL processes to be supported by portfolios: self-assessment, which can be informed internally via reflection and externally via feedback, goal-setting and planning, and monitoring". The framework guided both the design labelling of the eleven e-portfolio forms and the deductive codebook used in the content analysis, with reflection operationalised via Hatton and Smith's levels and goal-setting via Zimmerman's criteria.
requirements: Rating self-assessment directly was considered difficult to objectify, so the framework focuses on the two processes informing it, reflection and feedback
constraints: SRL is a comprehensive concept covering more processes than those considered, such as time management and self-efficacy
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning: reflection, feedback use, goal-setting and planning, and monitoring of learning
examples: The codebook for the content analysis was developed from this framework, using Hatton and Smith for reflection, Gibbs and Simpson for feedback, and Zimmerman for goal setting and planning

article_title: Relationship between students' perceptions of the adequacy of M1 and M2 curricula and their performance on USMLE step 1 examination.
citation: Khalil Mohammed K., Wright William S., Spearman Kelsey A., Gaspard Amber C. (2019). Relationship between students’ perceptions of the adequacy of M1 and M2 curricula and their performance on USMLE step 1 examination. BMC Medical Education 19:358. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1796-3
title: Collect student perceptions of curriculum adequacy shortly after a milestone licensing exam as a timely supplement to delayed score reports
description: The article proposes surveying students about whether the preclinical curriculum adequately covered exam content within weeks of the exam, because official performance analyses arrive late. The authors write that "receiving students’ feedback within two weeks of taking Step 1 examination is very helpful in making necessary changes to the curriculum for the upcoming academic year," whereas schools receive complete Step 1 analyses up to nine months later.
requirements: An anonymous survey administered within 2–3 weeks of the examination, combining closed-ended adequacy ratings with open-ended identification of insufficiently covered content areas
constraints: The study was conducted at one medical school using self-reported perceptions; individual-level correlation between perceptions and performance was not evaluated because the survey was anonymous
target_learners: second-year (M2) medical students preparing for USMLE Step 1
target_learning_goals: adequate curricular coverage of disciplines and organ systems tested on USMLE Step 1
examples: An anonymous survey with closed-ended and open-ended questions was sent to 174 medical students within 2–3 weeks of taking Step 1; results were shared with faculty at the annual curriculum retreat.

article_title: What Impedes General Practitioners' Identification of Mental Disorders at Outpatient Departments? A Qualitative Study in Shanghai, China.
citation: Zhang Hanzhi, Yu Dehua, Wang Zhaoxin, Shi Jianwei, Qian Jie. (2019). What Impedes General Practitioners’ Identification of Mental Disorders at Outpatient Departments? A Qualitative Study in Shanghai, China. Annals of Global Health. https://doi.org/10.5334/aogh.2628
title: Clarify GPs' diagnostic qualifications through policy and program support, combined with improved training and practice
description: The article argues that unclear qualification limited GPs' diagnosis of mental disorders, and that "Changes in policy and program supports are needed to make GPs’ qualification of diagnosis clear." Because GPs in developing countries lack knowledge, ability and confidence, such changes should focus both on improving the training and practice of mental disorder diagnostic procedures.
requirements: Policy and program supports that make GPs' diagnostic qualifications explicit, paired with training and practice of diagnostic procedures
constraints: The article notes further research is needed to determine application of these strategies and adjustments required in different developing countries
target_learners: General practitioners in developing countries with primary-stage healthcare systems
target_learning_goals: Competent diagnosis of mental disorders within general practice outpatient departments
examples: The article cites a 2014 Dutch mental health care reform under which patients with non-complex psychological problems should be recognized and treated within general practice.

article_title: Using poster presentation to assess large classes: a case study of a first-year undergraduate module at a South African university.
citation: Ross Andrew, Dlungwane Thembelihle, Van Wyk Jacqueline. (2019). Using poster presentation to assess large classes: a case study of a first-year undergraduate module at a South African university. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1863-9
title: Group poster presentation day as a large-class assessment pattern for community-service learning
description: A lesson/module-level design in which student groups of four design and co-present a poster about their community-service project to faculty assessors and peers at a scheduled poster day. At UKZN, "Sixty -three groups of four students each co-presented their work at the 'Making a Difference Poster Day', with an average of four groups being assessed per hour by two faculty assessors and their peers using a standardized marking rubric." Each group had 15 minutes (10-min presentation, 5-min questions), and the poster contributed 25% of the module mark.
requirements: Groups of four students with a shared project experience to present
A standardized marking rubric and paired faculty assessors
Scheduled presentation slots (15 min per group) within a poster day
constraints: Assessed a group product, so the same mark went to all group members, which only 60% of staff considered fair to individual contributors
target_learners: first-year undergraduate medical students in large classes
examples: 63 groups presented at the Making a Difference Poster Day in October 2018, assessed by 12 staff working in pairs over four hours
key_sources: Ross Andrew, Dlungwane Thembelihle, Van Wyk Jacqueline. (2019). Using poster presentation to assess large classes: a case study of a first-year undergraduate module at a South African university. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1863-9

article_title: Using poster presentation to assess large classes: a case study of a first-year undergraduate module at a South African university.
citation: Ross Andrew, Dlungwane Thembelihle, Van Wyk Jacqueline. (2019). Using poster presentation to assess large classes: a case study of a first-year undergraduate module at a South African university. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1863-9
title: Use poster presentations as an integrated teaching, assessment and feedback strategy in large classes
description: The article recommends poster presentations as a way to counter the engagement, assessment and feedback problems of massified large classes. In its conclusion it states: "Poster presentations should be more widely considered as an innovative way to encourage deeper engagement and learning in a large class setting." The recommendation rests on student and staff perceptions that posters promoted active engagement, higher-order synthesis, efficient marking and immediate feedback.
requirements: A product-based group task (e.g. community service) whose learning can be displayed on a poster
Faculty assessors, a standardized rubric, and timetabled presentation time
constraints: Evidence comes from one cohort in a resource-limited setting; the authors note educators elsewhere must judge applicability to their own settings
target_learners: large undergraduate classes in higher education, especially resource-constrained settings
examples: The MaD poster assessment at UKZN, where 250 first-year students were assessed via 63 group posters with immediate feedback in a four-hour session

article_title: Simulation of Urgent Airway Management in a Postthyroidectomy Hematoma.
citation: Wu Kitty, Kim Stephanie, Rajasingham Shihan J., Bruni Ida, Fung Kevin, Roth Kathryn E. (2019). Simulation of Urgent Airway Management in a Postthyroidectomy Hematoma. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10802
title: Postthyroidectomy hematoma simulation scenario for junior otolaryngology residents
description: A high-fidelity mannequin (SimMan 3G) simulation in which a 68-year-old male presents with an expanding cervical hematoma 2 hours after total thyroidectomy. Teams of three or four junior residents gather history, prioritize bedside hematoma decompression before operating-room arrangements, and manage confederates playing a ward nurse and an agitated family member. The article reports that "Since 2012, the simulation has been used with a total of 96 residents as part of an annual boot camp." The scenario runs 10 minutes for setup, 15–20 minutes for simulation, and 15 minutes for debriefing.
requirements: A high-fidelity mannequin such as the SimMan 3G, monitors, airway and tracheostomy equipment, and a low-cost hematoma moulage packet embedded in the mannequin's neck
Confederates playing a ward nurse and a family member, plus a guided debriefing session with guiding questions
constraints: Designed for junior residents (PGY 1, PGY 2) in otolaryngology–head and neck surgery or equivalent training levels
No formal assessment of medical judgments was designed, as the simulation was used in a formative setting
target_learners: Junior residents (PGY 1–2) in otolaryngology–head and neck surgery, anesthesiology, and other surgical specialties
target_learning_goals: Urgent airway management and bedside hematoma evacuation
Closed-loop communication and multidisciplinary team coordination in a crisis
examples: The hematoma packet was made with artificial blood from saline, red food coloring, and corn starch in a sealable plastic bag over craft foam
The SimMan's airway was set edematous and difficult but not impossible to intubate, worsening until the incision was released
key_sources: Wu Kitty, Kim Stephanie, Rajasingham Shihan J., Bruni Ida, Fung Kevin, Roth Kathryn E. (2019). Simulation of Urgent Airway Management in a Postthyroidectomy Hematoma. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10802

article_title: Podcasting in medical education: a review of the literature.
citation: Cho Daniel, Cosimini Michael, Espinoza Juan. (2017). Podcasting in medical education: a review of the literature. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2017.69
title: Medical education podcasts should be concise (roughly under 20 minutes) and meet quality standards of disclosure, attribution, accuracy, and accessibility
description: The review distills quality markers for educational podcasts from a modified Delphi study and related scoring systems (ALiEM AIR, METRIQ-8, METRIQ-5). Markers "include: disclosing conflicting interests, clearly identifying authors, clear distinction of fact versus opinion, accurate information, and accessibility". It also suggests podcasts be relatively concise, perhaps under 20 minutes, though no outcome-based length comparison exists.
requirements: Disclose conflicting interests; clearly identify authors; distinguish fact from opinion; ensure accurate, adequately cited, evidence-based content and accessibility
constraints: No one has reported a comparison of one length to another with regards to outcomes; 15 to 20 minutes is only a reasonable starting point
target_learning_goals: medical knowledge acquisition through audio podcast learning
examples: The review reports these criteria were developed to evaluate existing online educational resources and can guide development of new podcasts; general speaking guidance includes avoiding jargon and using shorter instead of longer words

article_title: Do portfolios have a future?
citation: Driessen Erik. (2016). Do portfolios have a future? Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-016-9679-4
title: Use portfolios as catalysts for mentor-learner dialogue: without mentoring, portfolios have no future
description: The article argues portfolios should operate through interaction between learner and supervisor, quoting the pioneers' definition of a system that operates "through the interaction of a learner and supervisor using the material as a catalyst to guide [discussion and] further learning." Twenty-five years of portfolio experience lead the author to conclude that without mentoring, portfolios are bureaucratic hurdles, and that mentoring is likely the most powerful learning method in the medical education toolbox.
requirements: Mentors with dedicated time for every learner who help learners use portfolio data to make sense of experiences and frame improvement plans
A trusting relationship between learner and mentor
constraints: Current learning environments and portfolios are strongly focused on accountability and checking, with unintended effects; mentor time is currently ensured only in the ideal world
examples: The author recommends establishing a portfolio that supports learning by guiding discussion between learner and mentor, with mentors helping frame plans for improvement, citing Eva et al. (2015)
key_sources: Driessen Erik. (2016). Do portfolios have a future? Advances in Health Sciences Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10459-016-9679-4

article_title: Massage and Storytelling Reduce Aggression and Improve Academic Performance in Children Attending Elementary School.
citation: Gonçalves Lia Lopes, Voos Mariana Callil, de Almeida Maria Helena Morgani, Caromano Fátima Aparecida. (2017). Massage and Storytelling Reduce Aggression and Improve Academic Performance in Children Attending Elementary School. Occupational Therapy International. https://doi.org/10.1155/2017/5087145
title: Address children's aggression with interventions that emphasize a positive model of respect and affection rather than punishment or authoritarian relationships
description: The article argues that aggressive behaviors in 6–8-year-old children are best addressed through school interventions built on positive relational models. It states that "Aggressive behaviors can be addressed in 6–8-year-old children by interventions that emphasize a positive model, of respect and affection", while "punishments and authoritarian relationships between children, teachers, and caregivers may not have such beneficial effects". Massage and storytelling classes are presented as concrete instances of such positive-model interventions.
requirements: Interventions emphasizing respect and affection, such as peer massage or storytelling classes, delivered within the school routine
constraints: The article links authoritarian approaches and activity based on adults' expectancies to possible resistance and aggression in children
target_learners: Elementary school children aged 6–8 years, including those with conduct problems
examples: The study's massage and storytelling extra classes, which promoted interaction, empathy, and self-regulation, served as the positive-model interventions

article_title: Contextual factors and clinical reasoning: differences in diagnostic and therapeutic reasoning in board certified versus resident physicians.
citation: McBee Elexis, Ratcliffe Temple, Picho Katherine, Schuwirth Lambert, Artino Anthony R. Jr., Yepes-Rios Ana Monica, Masel Jennifer, van der Vleuten Cees, Durning Steven J. (2017). Contextual factors and clinical reasoning: differences in diagnostic and therapeutic reasoning in board certified versus resident physicians. BMC Medical Education 17:211. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-017-1041-x
title: Post-encounter form (PEF) for assessing clinical reasoning
description: The post-encounter form is a computerized assessment instrument completed after each video encounter, which "collected additional requested information to include differential diagnosis, leading diagnosis with supporting data, and treatment plan." Each PEF was scored by two investigators using a previously established key, with entries assigned 0, 1 or 2 points, and inter-rater reliability was Kappa = 0.93. The article states its use "for assessment of clinical reasoning has been previously established in medical students."
requirements: A previously established scoring key agreed by a panel of expert physicians, and two investigators scoring with consensus resolution of disagreements.
constraints: The article states the PEF "represents one clinical reasoning outcome" and low correlations may partly reflect limited reliability of the outcome measures, including the use of self-assessment measures.
target_learning_goals: assessment of diagnostic and therapeutic clinical reasoning
examples: Participants completed a computerized PEF after each of three randomly ordered video encounters; missing data on the PEF were counted as incorrect.

title: The Postgraduate ME Model: a six-domain quality-assurance model for postgraduate medical e-learning
description: The Postgraduate ME Model is a working quality-assurance model for postgraduate medical e-learning built from an integrative review. "The domains of the model are preparation, software design and system specifications, communication, content, assessment, and maintenance", and "This model was partially based on the ISO-19796 standard, and drew on cognitive load multimedia principles". The review offers it as a practical framework for educators drafting e-learning strategies or evaluating e-learning initiatives.
requirements: The model's domains require validation with international experts and testing in controlled e-learning settings
constraints: Further analysis is required to determine the applicability of the model to audiences other than postgraduates
Fast-changing technology threatens to render the review's results obsolete

title: Preparation domain: define end users, authors, budgets and plans before building the e-learning platform
description: The preparation domain covers work completed "before designing and building the e-learning platform". The review describes it as "a two-step process" in which developers first define end users' platforms and expectations, then design the e-learning strategy to match users' knowledge, motivational level, skills, and expectations. "Twelve articles described the importance of knowing the end users", and authors should be selected for subject matter expertise.

E-learning authors should be selected based on subject matter expertise
constraints: Special functionalities for individuals with learning disabilities are incorporated only if applicable

target_learning_goals: needs analysis and planning for postgraduate medical e-learning programs

title: Design domain: reliable, secure, fast-access platforms with intuitive less-is-more navigation
description: The design domain concerns hardware and software choices that fit end users' needs. Most reviewed articles (n = 14) focused on "ready access to the e-learning platform" — fast, easy to find, and always available — and the review recommends testing across browsers, monitors and hand-held devices. Navigation should be user friendly and intuitive with a "less is more" design strategy.

A secure connection is needed to support privacy, legal, copyright and intellectual property requirements

citation: Schmidt Jessica N. MD, MPH; Kendall John MD; Smalley Courtney MD. (2015). Competency Assessment in Senior Emergency Medicine Residents for Core Ultrasound Skills. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.5811/westjem.2015.9.28587
title: Dual-method POC ultrasound competency assessment tool combining an OSCE checklist and a multiple-choice interpretation quiz
description: The article designed and implemented an assessment tool pairing an observed clinical skills exam (OSCE) with a computer-based multiple-choice quiz to evaluate "both image acquisition and image interpretation" in five core emergency medicine ultrasound applications (ECHO, aorta, FAST, pelvic, central line). Acquisition was scored by two independent US-trained emergency physicians using published checklists on a standardized patient, with a total possible score of 126 points; interpretation used a 38-question quiz with live cine-clips and still images compiled by an external server.
requirements: Two independent US-trained EM physician examiners completing a pre-defined OSCE checklist on a live standardized patient model
A computer-based multiple-choice quiz with normal and pathological images, compiled by an external server for de-identified scoring
constraints: The study used a small cohort of nine residents at a single urban academic institution
There is no recommendation for how many checklist items indicate competency or how scores correlate with clinical performance
examples: Nine senior residents each completed five OSCE-directed acquisition exams in 45 minutes and a 38-question interpretation quiz covering AAA, FAST, ECHO, pelvic and central line categories

title: Pair point-of-care diagnostic training with periodic supervision and skill-reinforcing resupply visits
description: The article concludes that half-day competency-based training with a field-tested job-aid equips community health workers to use diagnostics safely and accurately, but that occasional errors mean "supervisors should conduct periodic performance appraisals and make necessary corrections to ensure patient, CHW, and community safety." Supervision is framed as soon after training and then regular, with resupply visits doubling as opportunities for skill reinforcement in the CHW's normal environment.
requirements: CHWs must receive adequate training, job-aids, supplies, and follow-up supervision, as the article's conclusion states
constraints: Supervisory visits by health facility or district staff did not occur during the study period, and many CHWs had difficulty obtaining resupply from facilities

examples: Observers assessed CHWs at 3, 6, and 12 months post-training using a standardized checklist, and the article recommends a supervisor visit soon after training any new CHW cadre.

article_title: Live lecture versus video podcast in undergraduate medical education: A randomised controlled trial.
citation: Schreiber Benjamin E, Fukuta Junaid, Gordon Fabiana. (2010). Live lecture versus video podcast in undergraduate medical education: A randomised controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/1472-6920-10-68
title: Use video podcasts for reinforcement and revision rather than as replacements for live lectures
description: The article's concluding recommendation is that video podcasts "are not ready to replace traditional teaching methods, but may have an important role in reinforcing learning and aiding revision". This position rests on the trial's twin findings: equivalent short-term factual recall for podcasts and lectures, but a clear student preference for lectures and lower podcast ratings on engagement, presentation and content. Podcasts' convenience and playback-control advantages make them suitable complements for revision and catching up on missed sessions.
requirements: Matched or high-quality content and narration, with the same instructor and slides as equivalent lectures where possible
Availability on a freely accessible platform so students can watch at their convenience
constraints: Students found podcasts less engaging, requiring discipline and offering less motivation to complete
Knowledge was assessed only immediately after brief 15-minute interventions; longer-term retention was not tested
Participation was voluntary and out of hours, with drop-out creating potential selection and response bias
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in first clinical year
target_learning_goals: reinforcement of newly taught clinical content and revision for assessments
examples: In the trial, video podcasts were Powerpoint slides narrated by the same instructor with the same script as the live lecture, approximately 15 minutes each, watched individually with pause and rewind available
